passages.happening:
Ezekiel turns to Judah's neighbors. The Ammonites cried out in triumph when God's sanctuary was profaned, the land laid waste and Judah taken into exile (verse 3). ‘Because you clapped your hands and stomped your feet and rejoiced over the land of Israel with a heart full of contempt’ (verse 6), God will hand them over to the people of the east and cut them off (verses 4-7).

Moab and Seir said, ‘Look, the house of Judah is like all the other nations’ (verse 8). So God will open Moab's flank, its towns on the northern plateau, to the same people of the east, and they will know that he is the LORD (verses 9-11).
passages.hearers:
Ammon lay east of the Jordan, with its capital at Rabbah, modern Amman. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea; two of the towns named, Baal-meon and Kiriathaim, appear on the Mesha Stele, in which a Moabite king celebrated victories over Israel in the ninth century BC.

Clapping and stamping were gestures of mockery, the ancient equivalent of jeering at a fallen enemy. In a world of small rival kingdoms, rejoicing over a neighbor's fall, and taking advantage of it, was expected. The prophets treat it as a wrong that God sees.

Moab's taunt struck at Israel's identity. When Jerusalem fell, the neighbors concluded that Israel's God had failed like any other god. The refrain, that they will know he is the LORD, answers them: the fall was God's own judgment, not his defeat.
passages.later: Proverbs says, ‘Do not gloat when your enemy falls’ (Proverbs 24:17). Obadiah told Edom, ‘you should not gloat in that day, your brother’s day of misfortune’ (Obadiah 1:12).
passages.asks: Ammon clapped its hands when its neighbor fell. Ask whether you have ever been glad at someone else's downfall. And ask what it would look like to grieve instead.

passages.t: Edom and the Philistines, who took revenge
passages.happening:
‘Because Edom acted vengefully against the house of Judah, and in so doing incurred grievous guilt’ (verse 12), God will stretch out his hand against Edom from Teman to Dedan (verse 13). ‘I will take My vengeance on Edom by the hand of My people Israel’ (verse 14).

The Philistines too acted ‘with malice of soul to destroy Judah with ancient hostility’ (verse 15). God will cut off the Cherethites and the remnant along the coast (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
Edom, called Seir after its mountains, lay south of the Dead Sea, and its people were remembered as descendants of Esau, Jacob's brother. Edom was remembered for joining in when Jerusalem fell. The Philistines held the coastal plain to the southwest; the Cherethites were a people of that coast, linked with them.

The charge against both is revenge: they took the day of Judah's ruin as their chance to settle old scores.
passages.later: The psalm remembers that Edom said of Jerusalem, “Destroy it” (Psalm 137:7). The law says, ‘Vengeance is Mine; I will repay’ (Deuteronomy 32:35).
passages.hard:
Why does God promise to take vengeance on Edom by the hand of Israel, and is this chapter a license for national revenge?

Verse 14 says God will take his vengeance on Edom by the hand of his people Israel, and readers rightly ask whether the chapter approves one nation's revenge on another. Some see it fulfilled later, when in the second century BC the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus conquered Idumea, where Edomites had settled. Others read it more broadly, as a promise that Edom's hostility will not have the last word.

On the moral question, the chapter's own stress is that vengeance is God's, carried out according to his judgment, not Israel's private grudge. The nations are judged precisely for taking revenge and gloating. Scripture's wider teaching is that vengeance belongs to God and his people must not seize it. This chapter gives no warrant for any modern nation or people to claim to act as God's instrument against its enemies, and no people is a stand-in for any modern nation.
passages.asks: The nations were judged for taking revenge into their own hands. Ask whether there is someone you want to see paid back. And ask what it would mean to leave that judgment with God.
